---
title: "Missing values"
subtitle: "Bounced emails, uncoded replies and missing covariates"
bibliography: [../references.bib, ../references-new.bib]
---

```{r}
#| label: setup
#| include: false
# The estimator of the case, for spec_frame()
source("../R/housing/_tools.R")

# readr rather than datawizard::data_read(), which returns some empty cells as ""
audit <- readr::read_csv("../cases/housing/data/housing_audit.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)
```

This module of the [companion curriculum](index.qmd) is about the values that a data file does not hold, and about what each way of handling them does to an estimate. The housing-audit case comes from a field experiment by the original authors (OAs), who emailed public housing authorities across the United States from names meant to indicate a white, a Black or a Hispanic applicant and found that replies to the Hispanic names opened with the name of the sender less often [@EinsteinGlick2017DoesRaceAffect]; the [case study](../cases/housing/index.qmd) tells it in full. The public file of the OAs is unusually complete for a social-science dataset, yet it lacks three kinds of information, each for a different reason, and each kind enters the analysis at a different point. Every number on the page is computed when it is built, from the course file `cases/housing/data/housing_audit.csv`, whose construction the [module on building the analysis file](data-management.qmd) follows step by step.

## 1. Three kinds of missing information {#sec-kinds}

```{r}
#| label: counts
#| include: false
ref <- spec_frame(audit, comparison = "white", population = "replies", uncoded = "drop")
replies_wh <- audit |>
  datawizard::data_filter(reply == 1, group %in% c("white", "hispanic")) |>
  datawizard::data_modify(hisp = as.integer(group == "hispanic"))
n_sent <- nrow(audit)
n_bounced <- sum(is.na(audit$reply))
n_replies <- sum(audit$reply %in% 1)
n_uncoded <- sum(audit$reply %in% 1 & is.na(audit$named))
n_uncoded_wh <- sum(is.na(replies_wh$named))
n_thirds <- sum(is.na(audit$pop_third))
n_thirds_replies <- sum(is.na(audit$pop_third) & audit$reply %in% 1)
n_assess <- sum(is.na(audit$assessment_third))
```

@tbl-kinds sets out the three kinds, together with the third of each housing authority on the assessment score of the Department of Housing and Urban Development (HUD), which no specification of the curve uses but which is missing far more often than anything else in the file and so shows what the choices of section 5 can do when much is at stake. The last column counts the rows of the reference specification of the course, the coded replies to white and Hispanic names, that each kind of missing information touches.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-kinds
#| tbl-cap: "The kinds of missing information in the housing-audit data: how often each is missing in the file, when it arises in the experiment, and how many of the coded replies to white and Hispanic names, the rows of the reference specification, it affects. Source: `cases/housing/data/housing_audit.csv`."
#| echo: false
tibble::tibble(
  `Missing information` = c("Reply status of an email that bounced", "Greeting code of a reply",
                            "Community thirds of an authority", "HUD assessment third of an authority"),
  `In the file` = c(paste(n_bounced, "of", format(n_sent, big.mark = ","), "emails"),
                    paste(n_uncoded, "of", n_replies, "replies"),
                    paste(n_thirds, "of", format(n_sent, big.mark = ","), "emails"),
                    paste(n_assess, "of", format(n_sent, big.mark = ","), "emails")),
  `When it arises` = c("before any official read the email", "after the reply arrived",
                       "recorded about the authority, before the emails", "recorded about the authority, before the emails"),
  `Reference rows` = c("none: no bounced email is a reply",
                       paste(n_uncoded_wh, "replies left out of", nrow(replies_wh)),
                       paste(sum(is.na(ref$pop_third)), "of", nrow(ref)),
                       paste(sum(is.na(ref$assessment_third)), "of", nrow(ref)))
) |>
  tinytable::tt()
```

A fourth absence runs through the whole file and is of a different kind. The `r sum(audit$reply %in% 0)` delivered emails that drew no reply have no greeting at all, because a greeting exists only where a reply exists. Their greeting is not a value that was recorded and then lost, or one that a coder could not read, but an outcome that never came into being, and the problem that it raises, comparing greetings only among the emails that drew a reply, is a problem of design rather than of missing data. The [module on audit experiments](experiments.qmd#sec-posttreatment) and the [module on causal graphs](dags.qmd#sec-collider) take it up, and this page leaves it aside.

## 2. Why a value is missing {#sec-mechanisms}

What a missing value does to an estimate depends on why it is missing, and the vocabulary for the reasons goes back to @Rubin1976InferenceMissingData. In the review of @Little1992RegressionMissingXs, values are missing completely at random (MCAR) when the chance that a value is missing does not depend on any value in the data, observed or not, and missing at random (MAR) when it depends only on values that are observed (p. 1229). Values that are missing for reasons connected with what is missing, an income left blank because it is high, say, are missing not at random. Under MCAR the cases with complete data are a random subsample of all the cases, so an analysis of the complete cases alone loses precision but nothing else: "If the data are MCAR, listwise deletion will not introduce any bias into parameter estimates" [@Allison2009MissingData, p. 75], listwise deletion being the default of almost every statistical program, which drops every case with any missing value in the variables of a model.

An experiment adds a question that the three categories do not ask, namely whether the treatment could have changed whether a value is missing. @ZhaoDing2024AdjustNotAdjust put the point for covariates that are recorded before treatment: "the missingness indicators act as fully observed pretreatment covariates as long as missingness is not affected by the treatment" (abstract). A missingness indicator is a 0/1 variable that records, for each case, whether a value is missing, and the point of the sentence is that such an indicator, when it was settled before the treatment was assigned, is information about the cases like any other, which random assignment balances between the groups whether or not the values themselves are known. The last column but one of @tbl-kinds is there for this reason. The community thirds and the assessment third describe the authority and its community, from values measured by the census and by HUD, so the name cannot have changed whether the thirds are missing. A bounce is settled when the email fails to arrive, before any official could react to the name. The greeting codes are the exception, since the five uncoded replies were written by officials who had read the name, and whether a reply could be coded may in principle depend on what the name led the official to write.

## 3. Bounced emails {#sec-bounced}

Of the `r format(n_sent, big.mark = ",")` emails sent, `r n_bounced` bounced. They carry no reply status, since the codebook of the OAs records the reply as missing "if email bounced back due to email issue", and they never reached an official. The chunk below counts them by the group of the name and by whether the address was hard to find.

```{r}
#| label: bounced
audit |>
  datawizard::data_modify(bounced = as.integer(is.na(reply))) |>
  datawizard::data_summary(emails = n(), bounced = sum(bounced), share = 100 * mean(bounced), by = "group")

audit |>
  datawizard::data_modify(bounced = as.integer(is.na(reply))) |>
  datawizard::data_summary(emails = n(), bounced = sum(bounced), share = 100 * mean(bounced), by = "hard_email")

stats::chisq.test(table(audit$group, is.na(audit$reply)))$p.value  # r-style: keep – chisq.test() takes a table
```

```{r}
#| label: bounced-numbers
#| include: false
bounce_by <- audit |>
  datawizard::data_modify(bounced = as.integer(is.na(reply))) |>
  datawizard::data_summary(emails = n(), bounced = sum(bounced), share = 100 * mean(bounced), by = "group")
bounce_p <- stats::chisq.test(table(audit$group, is.na(audit$reply)))$p.value  # r-style: keep – chisq.test() takes a table
# With fewer than ten bounces for each name, the p-value of the test across the
# six names, each its own sending account, is simulated rather than read from
# the chi-square distribution
set.seed(20261105)
bounce_name_p <- stats::chisq.test(table(audit$name, is.na(audit$reply)), simulate.p.value = TRUE, B = 9999)$p.value  # r-style: keep – chisq.test() takes a table
# The twin of the menu page: every delivered email to a white or Hispanic name,
# an uncoded reply counted as not named, against every email sent, a bounced
# email counted as unanswered
delivered_twin <- spec_frame(audit, comparison = "white", population = "all", uncoded = "not_named")
all_sent <- audit |>
  datawizard::data_filter(group %in% c("white", "hispanic")) |>
  datawizard::data_modify(hisp = as.integer(group == "hispanic"),
                          y = dplyr::if_else(reply %in% 1, dplyr::coalesce(named, 0), 0))
gap_delivered <- 100 * stats::coef(stats::lm(y ~ hisp, data = delivered_twin))[["hisp"]]
gap_sent <- 100 * stats::coef(stats::lm(y ~ hisp, data = all_sent))[["hisp"]]
share_of <- bounce_by$share[match(c("white", "black", "hispanic"), bounce_by$group)]
```

The bounces are few and spread across the groups, at `r insight::format_value(share_of[1], digits = 1)`% of the emails with white names, `r insight::format_value(share_of[2], digits = 1)`% with Black names and `r insight::format_value(share_of[3], digits = 1)`% with Hispanic names, and a $\chi^2$ test finds no more difference between the groups than chance would produce (`r insight::format_p(bounce_p, stars = FALSE)`). For the name to have caused a bounce, a mail server would have had to refuse a message because of its sender. The counts by group give no reason to suspect such a refusal, but the counts by name are uneven: all the bounces among the white names came from Emily and none from Brett, and Tyrone had none either, a spread across the six names that chance would rarely produce (a $\chi^2$ test across the six names, with its p-value simulated because the counts are small, gives p = `r formatC(bounce_name_p, format = "f", digits = 3)`), so the sending account may have played a part. A bounced email is therefore best read as an email to which the treatment was never delivered, for reasons that no official could have influenced, and leaving the bounced emails out keeps the comparison among the delivered emails nearly as random as the assignment of the names made it, and every specification of the curve leaves the bounced emails out.

The alternative, counting a bounced email as one that went unanswered, matters only when all emails are counted, since a bounced email is never a reply. Among all delivered emails to white and Hispanic names, with the uncoded replies counted as not named, the gap in greetings by name is `r insight::format_value(gap_delivered, digits = 1, style_negative = "minus")` points. Counting the bounced emails as unanswered moves it to `r insight::format_value(gap_sent, digits = 1, style_negative = "minus")` points, a small change, but one produced by broken addresses rather than by officials, which is why the [specification menu](../cases/housing/menu.qmd#level-measurement) keeps the bounced emails off the curve.

## 4. Replies without a greeting code {#sec-uncoded}

The OAs coded the greeting of every reply but `r n_uncoded`, and the file does not say why these five were left uncoded.

```{r}
#| label: uncoded
audit |>
  datawizard::data_filter(reply == 1, is.na(named)) |>
  datawizard::data_select(c("email_id", "name", "group", "hard_email", "reply24"))
```

Three of the five went to white or Hispanic names, two to Emily and one to Santiago, and these three are the ones that can move the comparison of the claim. The specification menu offers two ways of handling the uncoded replies. Leaving them out is what a model does by default and what four of the five Multi100 analysts did. Counting them as replies that did not open with the name is a defensible reading, since a reply in which the coders found no greeting probably did not begin with one, and analyst 25N5D made that choice, without stating it, by keeping them in the counts of emails. Because the uncoded replies arose after the officials had read the name, neither option can lean on random assignment, and the safest check is one that assumes nothing about why the codes are missing. The two extreme codings provide it: all three named when the name was Hispanic and not named when it was white, which moves the gap as far towards zero as these replies can move it, and the reverse.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-uncoded
#| tbl-cap: "The gap in greetings by name between Hispanic and white names among the replies, under four codings of the three uncoded replies to these names: left out, counted as not named, and the two extreme codings. Differences in proportions with HC2 standard errors. Source: `cases/housing/data/housing_audit.csv`."
codings <- list(
  `left out` = datawizard::data_filter(replies_wh, !is.na(named)),
  `not named` = datawizard::data_modify(replies_wh, named = dplyr::coalesce(named, 0)),
  `named if Hispanic, not if white` = datawizard::data_modify(replies_wh, named = dplyr::coalesce(named, hisp)),
  `named if white, not if Hispanic` = datawizard::data_modify(replies_wh, named = dplyr::coalesce(named, 1 - hisp))
)
# dplyr inside the lambda, because datawizard does not see the arguments of a function
uncoded_gaps <- purrr::imap(codings, \(d, coding) {
  stats::lm(named ~ hisp, data = d) |>
    parameters::model_parameters(vcov = "HC2") |>
    dplyr::filter(Parameter == "hisp") |>
    dplyr::mutate(coding = coding, replies = nrow(d))
}) |>
  purrr::list_rbind()

uncoded_gaps |>
  datawizard::data_modify(gap = sub("^-", "−", sprintf("%.1f", 100 * Coefficient)),
                          se = sprintf("%.1f", 100 * SE)) |>
  datawizard::data_select(c(Coding = "coding", `Gap (points)` = "gap", SE = "se", Replies = "replies")) |>
  tinytable::tt() |>
  tinytable::style_tt(j = 2:4, align = "r")
```

Under every coding the gap stays between `r insight::format_value(max(100 * uncoded_gaps$Coefficient), digits = 1, style_negative = "minus")` and `r insight::format_value(min(100 * uncoded_gaps$Coefficient), digits = 1, style_negative = "minus")` points, so the uncoded replies cannot change the conclusion whatever their true greetings were. Bounds of this kind are the first check to run whenever an outcome is missing for a few cases, because such bounds need no assumption about why the values are missing and settle the question when the cases are few. With more missing outcomes the bounds would widen until they said nothing, and the analysis would then need an argument about why the outcomes are missing, the situation that the [trimming bounds of the module on audit experiments](experiments.qmd#sec-posttreatment) address for the emails without a reply.

## 5. Missing covariates {#sec-covariates}

The adjusted specifications of the curve add the hard-to-find address and the community thirds to the model, and these covariates are recorded before the emails went out. The names were assigned at random, so no covariate is needed to remove bias, and the adjustment serves only to narrow the standard error, as the [module on audit experiments](experiments.qmd#sec-randomisation) explains. A covariate that is missing for some authorities therefore raises a narrower question than it would in an observational study, namely how to keep the precision that the covariate offers without changing the comparison. The literature offers four answers to that question, which the rest of this section compares on the data of the case.

**Complete cases.** `lm()` drops every row with a missing value in any variable of the model, and the estimator of the course does the same, so the specifications that adjust for the community thirds rest on `r sum(!is.na(ref$pop_third))` of the `r nrow(ref)` coded replies of the reference comparison. @KingEtAl2001AnalyzingIncompletePolitical found that "approximately 94%" of the articles that they reviewed in political science used listwise deletion, "losing about one-third of their data, on average" (p. 49).

**Complete covariates.** An adjustment for the covariates that are observed for every authority, here the hard-to-find address alone, keeps every row. @ZhaoDing2024AdjustNotAdjust treat this as the baseline against which the other strategies are judged, since it is valid in a randomised experiment whatever the reason for the missing values.

**A category for the missing.** Each covariate with missing values receives one more category, or a 0/1 indicator, that marks the rows without it, and the model keeps every row. @Allison2009MissingData describes the method, for a categorical predictor, as one "whereby an extra category is created to hold the cases with missing data", and rejects it for regression on observational data, since a proof by Jones shows that it "typically produces biased estimates of the regression coefficients, even if the data are MCAR" (p. 76). @ZhaoDing2024AdjustNotAdjust reach the opposite recommendation for randomised experiments, for the reason given in section 2: when whether a covariate is missing was settled before the treatment, the indicator is a covariate recorded before treatment like any other, and adding it keeps the comparison of the experiment intact. They do not recommend the complete-case analysis there, which estimates the effect among the complete cases and so recovers the effect among all cases only if the two are the same (section 4.1).

**Multiple imputation.** Each missing value is replaced by a draw from a model that predicts it from the other variables, several times over, the analysis is run on each completed dataset, and the results are combined by the rules of Rubin, which add the variation between the completed datasets to the standard error. The mice package imputes variable by variable by chained equations, with a logit or a multinomial logit for a factor and predictive mean matching for a number by default [@BuurenGroothuis-Oudshoorn2011MiceMultivariateImputation, pp. 11, 22–23]. Its authors advise including in the imputation model "all variables that appear in the complete-data model, i.e., the model that will be applied to the data after imputation", the outcome included, since leaving them out "will tend to bias the results towards zero" (p. 22).

The community thirds are missing for only `r sum(is.na(ref$pop_third))` coded replies, so the four answers can differ only a little, and the chunk below fits the place adjustment of the curve (the hard-to-find address and the thirds of population and poverty) as complete cases and with a category for the missing.

```{r}
#| label: place
# The thirds as factors, and copies with a fourth level for the missing
frame <- ref |>
  datawizard::data_modify(.at = c("pop_third", "poverty_third", "assessment_third"),
                          .modify = \(x) factor(x, levels = c("lower", "middle", "top")))
frame_mi <- frame |>
  datawizard::data_modify(.at = c("pop_third", "poverty_third", "assessment_third"),
                          .modify = \(x) factor(dplyr::coalesce(as.character(x), "missing"),
                                                levels = c("lower", "middle", "top", "missing")))

place_fits <- list(
  `no adjustment, all replies` = stats::lm(y ~ hisp, data = frame),
  `no adjustment, complete cases` = stats::lm(y ~ hisp, data = datawizard::data_filter(frame, !is.na(pop_third))),
  `place set, complete cases` = stats::lm(y ~ hisp + hard_email + pop_third + poverty_third, data = frame),
  `place set, category for the missing` = stats::lm(y ~ hisp + hard_email + pop_third + poverty_third, data = frame_mi)
)
place <- purrr::imap(place_fits, \(fit, label) {
  parameters::model_parameters(fit, vcov = "HC2") |>
    dplyr::filter(Parameter == "hisp") |>
    dplyr::transmute(model = label, gap = 100 * Coefficient, se = 100 * SE, replies = stats::nobs(fit))
}) |>
  purrr::list_rbind()
place |> dplyr::mutate(dplyr::across(c("gap", "se"), \(x) round(x, 2)))
```

The complete-case adjustment moves the gap from `r insight::format_value(place$gap[1], digits = 1, style_negative = "minus")` to `r insight::format_value(place$gap[3], digits = 1, style_negative = "minus")` points, and the comparison of the first three rows shows that part of the move comes from dropping the five replies, before any covariate enters, since the unadjusted gap among the complete cases is already `r insight::format_value(place$gap[2], digits = 1, style_negative = "minus")` points. With a category for the missing, which keeps every reply, the adjusted gap is `r insight::format_value(place$gap[4], digits = 1, style_negative = "minus")` points. `lm()` reports one coefficient as not estimable in that model, because the same five replies lack both thirds, so a category for the missing in one third duplicates the category in the other, and R drops the duplicate.

The assessment third makes the difference between the answers visible, because it is missing for `r sum(is.na(frame$assessment_third))` of the `r nrow(frame)` coded replies, almost a third of them. It is also not missing completely at random, since the replies from authorities in the lower third of communities by population lack it far more often than those in the top third.

```{r}
#| label: assessment-pattern
frame |>
  datawizard::data_modify(assessment_missing = as.integer(is.na(assessment_third))) |>
  datawizard::data_summary(replies = n(), missing_share = 100 * mean(assessment_missing), by = "pop_third")

frame |>
  datawizard::data_modify(assessment_missing = as.integer(is.na(assessment_third))) |>
  datawizard::data_summary(named_share = 100 * mean(y), replies = n(), by = c("assessment_missing", "group"))
```

```{r}
#| label: assessment-gaps
#| include: false
by_missing <- frame |>
  datawizard::data_modify(assessment_missing = as.integer(is.na(assessment_third))) |>
  datawizard::data_summary(named_share = 100 * mean(y), by = c("assessment_missing", "group"))
# Hispanic minus white: the groups sort as hispanic, white
gap_complete <- by_missing |>
  datawizard::data_filter(assessment_missing == 0) |>
  datawizard::data_arrange("group") |>
  datawizard::data_extract("named_share") |>
  diff() * -1
gap_incomplete <- by_missing |>
  datawizard::data_filter(assessment_missing == 1) |>
  datawizard::data_arrange("group") |>
  datawizard::data_extract("named_share") |>
  diff() * -1
```

Among the replies from authorities with an assessment third, the gap between Hispanic and white names is `r insight::format_value(gap_complete, digits = 1, style_negative = "minus")` points, and among those without one it is `r insight::format_value(gap_incomplete, digits = 1, style_negative = "minus")` points. The difference may well be chance, since each group of replies is small, but it is exactly the situation in which a complete-case analysis changes what is estimated, because dropping the incomplete cases leaves the gap among the authorities that have an assessment score, not the gap among all the authorities that replied. The chunk below fits the adjusted model under four ways of handling the missing scores, beside the unadjusted gap, the last two being the interacted regression with a category for the missing that @ZhaoDing2024AdjustNotAdjust recommend, from `estimatr::lm_lin()`, and multiple imputation with mice, pooled with HC2 standard errors.

```{r}
#| label: assessment-fits
assess_fits <- list(
  `no adjustment, all replies` = stats::lm(y ~ hisp, data = frame),
  `no adjustment, complete cases` = stats::lm(y ~ hisp, data = datawizard::data_filter(frame, !is.na(assessment_third))),
  `assessment third, complete cases` = stats::lm(y ~ hisp + assessment_third, data = frame),
  `assessment third, category for the missing` = stats::lm(y ~ hisp + assessment_third, data = frame_mi)
)
assess <- purrr::imap(assess_fits, \(fit, label) {
  parameters::model_parameters(fit, vcov = "HC2") |>
    dplyr::filter(Parameter == "hisp") |>
    dplyr::transmute(model = label, gap = 100 * Coefficient, se = 100 * SE, replies = stats::nobs(fit))
}) |>
  purrr::list_rbind()

# The interacted regression of Zhao and Ding, with the covariate centred and
# interacted with the treatment, and HC2 errors
lin <- estimatr::lm_lin(y ~ hisp, covariates = ~ assessment_third, data = frame_mi, se_type = "HC2") |>
  estimatr::tidy() |>
  datawizard::data_filter(term == "hisp")

# Twenty imputations of every missing covariate from all the other columns,
# the outcome and the treatment included (van Buuren and Groothuis-Oudshoorn
# 2011, p. 22); each completed dataset fitted with HC2 errors and the results
# combined by Rubin's rules with mice::pool.scalar()
imputation_data <- frame |>
  datawizard::data_select(c("y", "hisp", "hard_email", "pop_third", "poverty_third", "assessment_third"))
imputed <- mice::mice(imputation_data, m = 20, seed = 20261105, printFlag = FALSE)
per_imputation <- purrr::map(seq_len(imputed$m), \(i) {
  stats::lm(y ~ hisp + assessment_third, data = mice::complete(imputed, i)) |>
    parameters::model_parameters(vcov = "HC2") |>
    dplyr::filter(Parameter == "hisp")
}) |>
  purrr::list_rbind()
pooled <- mice::pool.scalar(Q = per_imputation$Coefficient, U = per_imputation$SE^2,
                            n = nrow(imputation_data), k = 4)

assess <- dplyr::bind_rows(
  assess,
  tibble::tibble(model = c("interacted, category for the missing", "multiple imputation, 20 datasets"),
                 gap = 100 * c(lin$estimate, pooled$qbar), se = 100 * c(lin$std.error, sqrt(pooled$t)),
                 replies = nrow(frame))
)
```

```{r}
#| label: tbl-assessment
#| tbl-cap: "The gap in greetings by name between Hispanic and white names among the coded replies, adjusted for the HUD assessment third under four ways of handling its missing values, beside the unadjusted gap among all replies and among the complete cases. Linear probability models with HC2 standard errors; the imputations are combined by Rubin's rules. Source: `cases/housing/data/housing_audit.csv`."
#| echo: false
assess |>
  datawizard::data_modify(gap = sub("^-", "−", sprintf("%.1f", gap)), se = sprintf("%.1f", se)) |>
  datawizard::data_select(c(Model = "model", `Gap (points)` = "gap", SE = "se", Replies = "replies")) |>
  tinytable::tt() |>
  tinytable::style_tt(j = 2:4, align = "r")
```

Every strategy that keeps all `r nrow(frame)` replies gives a gap close to the unadjusted `r insight::format_value(assess$gap[1], digits = 1, style_negative = "minus")` points, from `r insight::format_value(max(assess$gap[c(4, 5, 6)]), digits = 1, style_negative = "minus")` to `r insight::format_value(min(assess$gap[c(4, 5, 6)]), digits = 1, style_negative = "minus")`, with standard errors of about `r insight::format_value(mean(assess$se[c(1, 4, 5, 6)]), digits = 1)` points. The complete-case analysis, by contrast, gives `r insight::format_value(assess$gap[3], digits = 1, style_negative = "minus")` points on `r assess$replies[3]` replies, with a larger standard error, and almost the whole of its departure is already present in the unadjusted gap among the same complete cases. The adjustment itself changes little. Dropping the authorities without a score changes the comparison, and it costs the precision that the adjustment was meant to buy.

Multiple imputation adds almost nothing here. The share of the variance of the gap that comes from the variation between the imputations, which mice reports as the fraction of missing information, is `r insight::format_value(pooled$fmi, digits = 3)`, because the name was assigned at random and so carries no information about the missing scores, whatever they are. In an experiment the category for the missing gives the same answer with no model of the missing values, which is the case made by @ZhaoDing2024AdjustNotAdjust for preferring it. Imputation earns its place where the variable with missing values is itself the object of the analysis rather than an aid to precision: a comparison of the gap across the thirds of percent Hispanic, which the [subgroups module](subgroups.qmd) sets out, cannot give the replies without a third a category of their own, and an observational comparison, such as one among the officials who replied, has no random assignment to fall back on. There, the observational case argued by @Allison2009MissingData and by @KingEtAl2001AnalyzingIncompletePolitical applies in full, and the plausibility of MAR, here a missing score explained by the size of the community and the other recorded columns, becomes the assumption on which the estimate depends.

## 6. Missing values on the curve {#sec-curve}

Each kind of missing information enters the curve of the case in its own way. The bounced emails are outside the experiment under every option, because no official read a bounced email. The uncoded replies are a decision of the menu, left out or counted as not named, and the two extreme codings of section 4 show that no handling of them can change the conclusion. The community thirds are handled as complete cases, so the specifications that adjust for them lose `r sum(is.na(ref$pop_third))` of the `r nrow(ref)` coded replies of the reference comparison, and part of the shift between the adjusted and the unadjusted specifications, as the [specification menu](../cases/housing/menu.qmd#level-estimation) notes, comes from the rows that the adjustment loses rather than from the adjustment itself. A declared analysis can name a different handling, such as a category for the missing, provided that the declaration names it before the model is run, since a choice made after the estimates are known is one more of the forking paths of the [multiverse module](multiverse.qmd).

::: {.callout-tip}
## Try it

Fit the specification of the curve with the fullest adjustment (the hard-to-find address and the thirds of population, poverty, percent Black and percent Hispanic) as complete cases with `fit_spec(audit, adjust = "place_ethnic")`, then with a category for the missing in each third, and decide how much of the difference between the two comes from the five dropped replies. Then rerun the imputation with `m = 5` and two different seeds, and compare the pooled gaps and their standard errors with those in @tbl-assessment. Finally, write the sentence of a preregistration that states how your declared analysis handles each of the three kinds of missing information of @tbl-kinds.
:::

## Sources and further reading {#sec-sources}

The terms of section 2 come from @Rubin1976InferenceMissingData, and @Little1992RegressionMissingXs reviews the methods for regression with missing covariates; @Allison2009MissingData is a short, clear introduction to listwise deletion, the methods that replace a missing value with a guess, maximum likelihood and multiple imputation. The case for the missing-indicator method in randomised experiments, and against complete cases there, is made by @ZhaoDing2024AdjustNotAdjust, under assumptions about nothing but the random assignment. Multiple imputation in political science is set out by @KingEtAl2001AnalyzingIncompletePolitical, and the mice package by its authors [@BuurenGroothuis-Oudshoorn2011MiceMultivariateImputation]. The construction of the course file, with the checks of its missing values, is in the [module on building the analysis file](data-management.qmd), and the counts of every column are in the [codebook of the course file](../cases/housing/data/housing_audit_codebook.md).
